job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I get up late, honestly, around nine, because the applications don't open until companies wake up anyway. I live with my mum and my little sister Ayo in a flat above a bakery on Mill Road. I send a few applications, read job boards, then walk to the library because the flat is loud. I finished electrical engineering at Brackenridge University in June, and my final project was a solar controller for a community garden's water pump.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. And what did you do for your internship, and what are you hoping for now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spent six weeks in the street lighting team at the city council, checking lamp records and helping an engineer called Mr Okafor test sensor boxes. It was good, a real workplace, and I liked it. Now I'm hoping for a graduate job in power or infrastructure, something public or at least unionised, where people are treated properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, nothing to panic about, but it doesn't help me today. I've applied to forty places and my inbox is mostly automatic rejections. To friends I'd probably joke that the robots can't even reject me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I still feel stuck. Plenty of jobs exist near me, so the problem is that thousands of graduates chase each one. My savings give me about eight months, and I do count them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but ten a week instead of three, and I'd ask Mr Okafor at the council whether any apprenticeship-style graduate scheme opens next spring. I'd also finally go to the careers office, which I've avoided. I wouldn't touch AI tools for my applications, I'd rather write them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly uneasy, not frightened. My money is fine, but every week without an offer makes me doubt my degree a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid AI tools even for applications. Does that cost you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Friends say the tools tidy up a CV in minutes, and I spend an evening on one. But I want my own words on it, and I don't trust something I can't see inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the slow search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that cut graduate schemes to save money and then complain about a skills shortage. I blame them, not the other graduates.

say: I'd tell friends this is **fine**, but it doesn't solve my search today.
I'd joke that robots can't even write my rejection emails properly.
think: I still feel **stuck**, because thousands of graduates apply for each opening near me.
My savings give me about **eight months**, and I count them often.
do: Apply to **ten jobs a week** instead of three.
Ask Mr Okafor (my council mentor) about a graduate scheme next spring.
Visit the university **careers office** I've been avoiding.
feel: **Uneasy**, not frightened: money is fine, but each empty week makes me doubt my degree.
S0.quote: Plenty of jobs exist near me, so the problem is that thousands of graduates chase each one.
fieldNote: His money is safe, yet the **unanswered** job hunt alone keeps him uneasy.
Avoids AI tools on **principle**, and admits it may cost him time.
Blames **employers** cutting graduate schemes, not other graduates.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to power and infrastructure employers
Book a careers office session about graduate schemes
Ask the council mentor about next spring's scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sign companies will use this to cut the entry rung of the ladder, and that governments must set rules now. At a union meeting I'd ask who retrains the people whose tasks get moved to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Entry-level engineers do a lot of checking, drawing and drafting, which is exactly what the card says goes first. So fewer graduate posts, more applicants. I'd be one of the ones squeezed, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to site-based roles like commissioning and testing, where someone has to physically be there. I'd join the graduate section of the engineers' union for advice and CV reviews. I'd also try one AI drawing tool, reluctantly, because an interviewer will ask about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still have control, I have my savings and my mum's flat, but I can see the door narrowing, and that's tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said reluctantly try one tool. What would make you stop being reluctant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a union-agreed rule that it's used to help people, not to replace them. If my employer says it frees me for design work and puts that in writing, I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home if the search drags on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my mum would hide it from me, but I'd stop my phone upgrade, the gym, and the Saturday bus trips to see friends. My sister's school trip stays, I'd pay for that.

say: I'd say companies will use this to cut **entry-level** posts, and governments must set rules now.
At the union I'd ask who pays to **retrain** people whose tasks move to software.
think: Checking and drafting are my entry-level tasks, so I'd be **squeezed** by fewer posts and more applicants.
I know it, and I try not to look at the numbers.
do: Widen my search to **site-based** commissioning and testing roles.
Join the engineers' union graduate section for CV reviews.
Try **one AI drawing tool**, because interviewers will ask.
feel: **Anxious** but in control: I can see the door narrowing, and that's tiring.
S1.quote: If my employer says it frees me for design work and puts that in writing, I'd use it.
fieldNote: Reads the card through a union lens and asks who pays for **retraining**.
Would use AI only with a written, **employer-backed** promise it supports workers.
**Protects** his sister's school trip before his own spending.

steps.text: Look for site commissioning and testing roles near home
Join the engineers' union graduate section
Try one AI drawing tool before interviews
Stop the phone upgrade and Saturday bus trips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a joke. I'd say publicly that this is reckless and that governments have to slow it down and protect jobs before anything else. I'd sign anything and march if the union called it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. Everything I trained for is thinking work, and by 2028 a machine does the thinking work cheaper, so who hires a first-year engineer? Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so the site jobs hold a few extra years, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for the perfect offer and take anything in engineering, even a technician job. I'd move my savings into a safe account and not spend any of it. I'd also push my mum to keep her hospital job and give her my share of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake with this. I can't see how my family copes if both of us lose income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd march. What would you actually want the government to do in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay people a living income while they retrain, and make companies share what they save. Not a tiny handout, a proper one, and tax the firms that profit from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your degree still have any value in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As a piece of paper, less. As knowing how power and circuits really work, maybe more, because someone has to check the machines. I just can't be sure.

say: Two years is **reckless**; governments must slow it and protect jobs first.
I'd sign any petition and march if the **union** called it.
think: Everything I trained for is thinking work, so I'm **scared** nobody hires a first-year engineer.
Site jobs may hold a few extra years, but **not forever**.
do: Take **any engineering job**, even technician work, instead of waiting.
Move my savings to a **safe account** and stop spending.
Give my mum my share of the rent so she keeps her hospital job.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless: I can't see how my family copes if we both lose income.
S2.quote: By 2028 a machine does the thinking work cheaper, so who hires a first-year engineer?
fieldNote: Fear shows under the protest **language**, and he admits it only off the record.
Drops his picky job search for any **technician** role.
Wants a **living** income and a tax on firms that profit.

steps.text: Accept any technician or engineering job offered within weeks
Move savings into a safe account and freeze spending
Join union marches and petitions about AI
Press the government for a living income while retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives time, but it's still too fast for the people who run things. I'd say the unions, the government and the universities should start now, and I'd say it loudly at the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is probably enough to get a job and a few years' experience, so I'd hold a position when it arrives. But I'd be in my twenties with a mortgage idea and not much else. That's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for a first job within six months, preferably public sector, which usually moves slower on new technology. Then I'd spend evenings on a part-time master's in power systems, because grid work needs people physically responsible. I'd keep saving most of what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier than the two-year one. There's something to do, and having something to do helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why public sector specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Public sector answers to voters, so cutting jobs fast is harder, and that's more of a promise than a private firm gives. I know it isn't a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister, who is fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study something where you have to be in the room, like nursing or electrics, and still learn how to think. And don't believe anyone who says they know how this ends.

say: Five years is **still too fast** for governments and universities, and I'd say so loudly.
think: Five years may be enough to land a job and **hold a position**.
I'd still be young with little behind me, and that bothers me.
do: Get a **first job** within six months, preferably in the public sector.
Start a part-time **master's in power systems** in the evenings.
Keep saving most of my pay.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, because having a plan helps.
S3.quote: Public sector answers to voters, so cutting jobs fast is harder, and that's more of a promise than a private firm gives.
fieldNote: Treats public-sector work as the **slowest-moving** safe harbour.
Plans further study but only **alongside** a job, not instead of one.
Thinks of his **fifteen-year-old** sister's future before his own.

steps.text: Apply for council and utility graduate roles first
Enrol in an evening master's in power systems
Save two-thirds of every pay cheque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like a bearable amount of time, and I'd say treat ten years as a deadline, not a comfort, because governments waste a decade very easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's quite calm. By then I'd have a career behind me, perhaps with grid or infrastructure work, which robots reach about three years after the thinking work. I'd worry for my sister and for people who are slow to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the normal route, a first job and then chartered status, and I'd back the union's campaign for a shared training fund. Maybe around thirty I'd think about a switch to something like control systems. I'd keep living cheaply with family until I buy a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd be annoyed at the politicians, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said treat it as a deadline. What would you want in place by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A training fund every employer pays into, and a clear public list of which jobs are at risk. I want the information, so people don't find out on a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having time make you more willing to try AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. If I have years to learn it with colleagues around me, I'd do it. It's being thrown in that I hate.

say: Ten years should be treated as a **deadline**, not a comfort.
Governments waste a decade very easily, so I'd press them early.
think: For me it feels **bearable**: I'd have a career built before robots reach site work.
I'd worry more for my **sister** and slower people.
do: Take a first job, then work towards **chartered engineer** status.
Back the union's call for a shared **training fund**.
Think about a switch to **control systems** around thirty.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, and annoyed at politicians rather than frightened.
S4.quote: Treat ten years as a deadline, not a comfort, because governments waste a decade very easily.
fieldNote: Time lowers his fear **sharply** and makes him willing to learn tools.
Wants public **information** on which jobs are at risk.
His worry shifts from **himself** to his sister and slower movers.

steps.text: Take a first job and aim for chartered engineer status
Campaign for an employer-funded training fund through the union
Learn AI drawing tools alongside colleagues in a few years
Keep living with family until buying a small flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I can plan for five or ten years, I can't plan for two, and my mum's cleaning hours at the hospital wouldn't cover the flat if I'm stuck. Even with my savings, two years is just not enough time for anyone to get ready, least of all me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me get told to just learn the tools. I'm not against progress, I'm against being rushed and then blamed. If a company wants me to change, they should train me and pay me while I do it.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress, I'm against being rushed and then blamed.
portrait: Femi is a **23-year-old** electrical engineering graduate living with his mum and sister, still waiting for a first offer after several months.
He is **progressive** and union-minded, and he blames companies and weak rules rather than himself or the technology.
He **avoids AI tools** and likes slow, proven change, so he leans on his savings and family while he waits.
His mood climbs with speed: **uneasy** when little changes, anxious when entry-level work shrinks, alarmed when it happens in two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because there would be no time to prepare and nobody ready to help.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** from employers and strong **public support**, with rules that slow things down enough for people to adapt.
